#6049. Trump says Israel will stop receiving $4B in US aid by year's end, can still buy weapons

President Donald Trump joins 'Fox & Friends' to deliver a final Election Day message as voters cast their ballots in the high-stakes midterms. Trump discusses his record, the state of the Middle East and other top issues.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. aid to Israel would end at the close of the year, arguing that the country no longer needs the assistance and can purchase its own weapons.

"We were giving them $4 billion – we are – but it gets cut off at the end of the year," Trump told "Fox & Friends" on Tuesday in an Election Day morning announcement.

Trump acknowledged the political nature of the news, pointing to Michigan's battleground Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought a zero aid proposal to President Donald Trump, who makes the stunning announcement on midterm Election Day morning on "Fox & Friends." (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it?" Trump said. "It's a bad talking point."

The support included "things and money," according to Trump, calling it military aid, cash or "barter." He said he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed ending the assistance for years, adding that Netanyahu raised the idea.

"They don’t need it," Trump said. "Israel's our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it."

"Israel is a very thriving country," he added.

NETANYAHU DETAILS 'FINAL' CONVERSATION WITH LINDSEY GRAHAM, SAYS SENATOR CHALLENGED HIS PUSH TO END ISRAEL AID

The current U.S.-Israel security assistance agreement provides about $3.8 billion annually through 2028. Netanyahu has previously said he wants to phase out Israel’s reliance on U.S. military aid, though the timing and terms of any change to the agreement have not been detailed.

Trump said the assistance had become a political target, adding that Netanyahu understood "this is one of their points of contention."

"If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen because America has changed," Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in October.

The $4 billion referred to military hardware or cash, according to Trump.

NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's aggressive anti-Israel aid stance against Republican Mike Rogers might have been a factor in President Donald Trump's Election Day-timed announcement Tuesday. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images; Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"I’m going to put it in any way you want to define it," Trump said. "You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash. It’s what we give them — $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it."

Trump negotiated the new deal with Netanyahu, who is also facing a difficult election season with his future still up in the air as the balance of power in the Knesset tries to settle on a coalition government amid multifront wars with terrorists and Iran.

"I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money," he said. "He brought it up. He said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.’"

EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY

Congress passed a law in 2020 authorizing the funding for Israel, but the Senate and House must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.

Israel can still buy U.S. weapons, Trump stressed.

"They can buy whatever they want," he said.

SEN RAND PAUL: OUR BUDGET DEFICIT IS OUT OF CONTROL. CONGRESS MUST PASS MY SIX PENNY PLAN

Trump pointed to his administration's 2024 campaign vows to curb free foreign aid and cut government spending, just hours before the balance of congressional power will be determined for his final two years in office.

"We've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money," Trump said. "You know, somebody that wants to have a balanced budget. I'd love to be able to balance our budget."

"If we had a fed that got interest rates down," he added, "we would have a balanced budget quickly. It's a shame, the interest rates. We have a fed that's, you know, populated by Obama and Biden people, and they don't want to do the right thing."

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

#6047. The Quiet Revolution in U.S.-Cypriot Relations

Analysis: The Quiet Revolution in U.S.-Cypriot Relations

Since the 1974 Turkish invasion of Cyprus, Washington has almost exclusively seen the island as a problem in need of solution. But that dynamic has now quietly changed. Over the past decade, the Republic of Cyprus (ROC) has positioned itself as a critical security partner for an increasingly receptive United States. The bilateral relationship has gradually expanded to include defense, trade, basing, military training and exercises, crisis-response cooperation, and regular strategic dialogue. Given Cyprus’s strategic location, it is perhaps surprising that the initial impetus for this growing security relationship came from Cyprus, not Washington.

In short, despite its ongoing division, Cyprus is emerging as a security producer for the United States and the West. For Nicosia, this relationship serves as an effective deterrent against any future Turkish threat, which remains the ROC’s primary security preoccupation. Beyond that, deepening ties with the United States help boost Cyprus’s international status and provide cover for its growing arms relationships and other security ties with other states, such as France and Israel. Turkey has watched these developments warily, though so far without a forceful response.

Since the 1974 Turkish invasion of Cyprus, Washington has almost exclusively seen the island as a problem in need of solution. But that dynamic has now quietly changed. Over the past decade, the Republic of Cyprus (ROC) has positioned itself as a critical security partner for an increasingly receptive United States. The bilateral relationship has gradually expanded to include defense, trade, basing, military training and exercises, crisis-response cooperation, and regular strategic dialogue. Given Cyprus’s strategic location, it is perhaps surprising that the initial impetus for this growing security relationship came from Cyprus, not Washington.

In short, despite its ongoing division, Cyprus is emerging as a security producer for the United States and the West. For Nicosia, this relationship serves as an effective deterrent against any future Turkish threat, which remains the ROC’s primary security preoccupation. Beyond that, deepening ties with the United States help boost Cyprus’s international status and provide cover for its growing arms relationships and other security ties with other states, such as France and Israel. Turkey has watched these developments warily, though so far without a forceful response.

Since 1974, the ROC has governed only the island’s southern two-thirds while enjoying near-universal recognition as the de jure government of the entire island (other than two sovereign British bases constituting less than 3 percent of the island). Turkey occupies the island’s northern third, which declared independence in 1983 as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC). Only Turkey recognizes the TRNC, and its military is believed to maintain 30,000-40,000 troops there. The overwhelmingly Greek Cypriot population of ROC-held territory numbers just under a million; the Turkish Cypriot population in the north is about a quarter that size.

During the Cold War, the ROC joined the Non-Aligned Movement as a founding member in 1961 and remained in the group until it joined the European Union in 2004, which forced it to abandon formal neutrality. Maintaining reasonably good ties with both Washington and Moscow made sense, as both permanent members of the U.N. Security Council would influence any settlement of the island’s division.

Even after securing EU membership, Cyprus’s ties to Moscow initially remained close. The United States, for its part, was wary of pursuing security ties with the ROC. Concerned that close relations with Cyprus would upset the Turks and jeopardize prospects for Cypriot reunification, Washington went so far as to put an arms embargo on the country in 1987.

Cyprus’s East-West balancing act began to change significantly in 2013, when the ROC elected the pro-Western Nicos Anastasiades as president, replacing his Moscow-friendly, anti-NATO predecessor, Demetris Christofias of the communist Progressive Party of Working People. Rather than wait for another attempt at reunification to transform Cyprus’s geopolitical position, Anastasiades sought to build a U.S.-Cypriot relationship. He pitched Washington on the island’s strategic location at the intersection of Europe and the Middle East, with ports, airfields, offshore energy resources, and diplomatic ties across the region.

Washington, perhaps increasingly skeptical that decades-old reunification efforts would ever bear fruit, responded in kind to Cypriot overtures. By 2014, then-Vice President Joe Biden had publicly described the bilateral relationship as a “strategic partnership.”

This mutual shift in outlook accelerated during the first Trump administration, likely reinforced by the collapse of the most recent diplomatic effort at reunification in July 2017. The result was a 2018 bilateral statement of intent that laid the groundwork for future security cooperation. The U.S. Congress followed with the 2019 Eastern Mediterranean Security and Energy Partnership Act, which formally declared Cyprus a “key strategic partner” and created a path toward suspending the 1987 U.S. arms embargo.

For the United States, the opening reflected a reconceptualization of the region, accelerated by a worsening relationship with Turkey in the 2010s.

Former Assistant Secretary of State for Eurasian Affairs A. Wess Mitchell, widely viewed as the chief architect of the shift, argued in 2018 congressional testimony that Washington’s thinking about the region had grown stale. The United States, he said, had for decades mistakenly treated the Eastern Mediterranean as settled terrain anchored by Turkey while reducing Cyprus merely to a matter of reunification talks. In Mitchell’s vision, the Eastern Mediterranean was an “emerging maritime frontier” warranting greater attention. Greece and Cyprus, he reasoned, offered the United States strategic opportunities while also providing a hedge against an increasingly erratic Turkey.

For Cyprus, however, the reason for turning toward Washington wasn’t merely strategic; it was existential. Nicosia was seeking a suspension of Washington’s arms embargo, but more than that, it wanted a sense of strategic belonging. As the lone EU member outside both NATO and NATO’s Partnership for Peace program, which allows non-NATO governments to build a bilateral relationship with the alliance, Cyprus has tried to shed its status as Europe’s “half-in” member.

The ROC’s president, Nikos Christodoulides, has gone beyond his predecessors in that regard, saying repeatedly that he wants Cyprus inside NATO. Christodoulides knows that, given Turkey’s veto, that is a nearly inconceivable prospect absent a Cyprus settlement agreement. Nevertheless, he has cast cooperation with Washington as a means of bringing the Cypriot National Guard, as the Cypriot army is called, up to alliance standards.

Cooperation with the United States has helped professionalize the Cypriot military and upgrade Cyprus’s military infrastructure. Cypriot and American troops now train together, including by conducting special operations exercises beyond emergency rescue drills. U.S. Navy SEALs and the Cypriot navy’s underwater team conducted joint maritime counterterrorism and ship-boarding training in 2021 and 2024. Since 2022, Cyprus has partnered with the New Jersey National Guard for joint training and disaster response. In December 2024, Congress made Cyprus eligible for U.S.-financed multilateral training—the only non-NATO, non-Partnership for Peace country with this status.

Through the U.S. European Command (EUCOM), Washington funded a roughly $588,000 assessment in 2025 to bring Andreas Papandreou Air Base up to NATO standards, recommending a new heavy-lift apron and expanded runway, which Cyprus will finance. A new EUCOM-funded heliport at Evangelos Florakis Naval Base will accommodate large Chinook-type helicopters, and the Ministry of Defense is studying expansion to host eight large warships. Limassol has become a routine U.S. Navy port of call, hosting 22 vessels since 2022, including 15 since 2024.

Cyprus has expanded its cooperation with the United States by taking on regional responsibilities that leverage its strategic location while seeking to avoid provoking Turkey. The country’s national plan enables rapid noncombatant evacuation, opening ports and airports for civilians fleeing conflicts. In 2024, U.S. Marines and Ospreys deployed to Papandreou Air Base for possible evacuations from Lebanon, and Cyprus served as a transit point for those leaving Israel during the June 2025 Iran conflict.

Beyond evacuations, Cyprus has supported humanitarian deliveries to Gaza in partnership with the U.N., sending more than 37,000 metric tons of supplies. Its location at the crossroads of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East has also made it a regional training hub. By 2025, the U.S.-funded Cyprus Center for Land, Open Seas, and Port Security  in Larnaca had trained more than 2,000 officials from more than 20 countries in security and counterterrorism.

Of course, the question of Turkey is never far from Cypriot calculations. Closer ties to Washington plainly serve Nicosia’s concerns about its neighbor.

An example of how U.S. ties provide indirect deterrence is found in Cyprus’s recently acquired air-defense capability. When Cyprus sought to field Russian S-300 air-defense missiles in 1997, Ankara threatened to bomb the batteries before they were fully deployed. Washington defused that crisis by pressing Nicosia to transfer the S-300s to Greece, which then stored them unobtrusively on Crete.

When Cyprus purchased the Israeli Barak MX system in 2024, however, Turkey warned of dangerous consequences but never threatened direct military intervention to block Cyprus from deploying it. Several factors may explain Turkey’s more restrained response in 2024, but Cyprus’s new security relationship with the United States, including the limited but consistent presence of U.S. troops in the ROC, is certainly among the most important.

Meanwhile, Israel also has emerged as a key security partner for Cyprus. Although Cyprus’s security relationship with Israel predates the acceleration of its security ties with Washington, the latter has accelerated expansion of the former.

Beyond bilateral Israeli-Cypriot relations, Cyprus, Israel, and Greece hold regular joint summits and cooperate in several areas, including energy. That triangular relationship has made the Turks uneasy, but the United States has blessed it and, since Trump’s first term, occasionally participates in it, creating a grouping known as the “3+1.” Cyprus has also built important ties with other regional actors, including Egypt, Jordan, and several Persian Gulf states.

This emerging strategy carries risks for both Washington and Nicosia. The island now hosts more arms than at any point in decades, and each proposed U.S. transfer forces a judgment about whether additional weaponry and military infrastructure projects bolster stability or erode it. Perhaps tellingly, Washington has yet to act on a Cypriot request for excess defense articles made more than a year ago.

The broader challenge for the United States is to draw on Cyprus’s location and strengthen its military without stoking Turkish fears to the point of reigniting long-dormant hostilities, an outcome that is squarely against U.S. interests. For Cyprus, the corresponding danger is losing control over a relationship with a far more powerful partner, as a U.S. military increasingly comfortable operating from the island may eventually seek to stage operations from it, drawing the ROC into conflicts that it would prefer to avoid. Conversely, Cyprus has to reckon with the possibility that a more isolationist United States might abandon the security relationship altogether.

Cyprus’s deepening ties with Israel sharpen that exposure. As relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated since Oct. 7, 2023, Cyprus risks becoming another arena of Turkish-Israeli friction, alongside Syria and the Horn of Africa.

Closer alignment with Washington and Israel also draws the island nearer to the confrontation with Iran: In March 2026, a drone most likely launched by Hezbollah from Lebanon struck a sovereign British base in the island’s south, just a few miles from ROC territory—a reminder that Cyprus can be targeted in conflicts not of its own making. Nicosia must therefore work to keep Israeli-Turkish tensions, and the wider Iranian threat, from boiling over onto the island.

Nicosia wants Washington to see it as a natural ally, even absent a treaty to that effect, as well as a security producer rather than a divided country whose enduring security problem overwhelms all other considerations. To that end, it has positioned itself as a friendly, democratic government in a tough region that can help evacuate Americans from Middle Eastern wars, train regional security officials, host naval vessels, support humanitarian missions, counter illicit finance, obstruct terrorism, and operate alongside Western militaries.

Still, that transformation remains incomplete. Cyprus may be an unsinkable aircraft carrier, but the United States is still deferential to Turkish sensibilities regarding Cyprus, even if it is much less deferential than it was a decade ago, and for now has not sought to exploit Cyprus’s full military potential. Cyprus, too, likes to emphasize that it does not allow foreign militaries to stage offensive operations from its territory, a position most recently reiterated at the outset of the Iran war.

Cyprus is not a formal U.S. ally, hosts no permanent U.S. bases, and remains outside NATO. The island’s unresolved division will likely continue to constrain how far military cooperation with the United States can go. Should the prospect of reunification vanish altogether, the strategic ambiguity that has allowed the partnership to deepen quietly may grow harder to sustain, pressing Washington to weigh Cypriot opportunity against Turkish sensitivities more openly than it has so far.

But Nicosia no longer appears willing to let that dispute define the boundaries and ambition of its foreign policy. After decades of waiting for geopolitics to change its circumstances, Cyprus is now actively using its geography and growing strategic importance to change its geopolitics.

Alan Makovsky is a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, a Washington-based think tank. He was formerly an official at the State Department and a senior staff member at the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Jonah Brody is a policy analyst at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America.

#6045. 9th Circuit block on California noncitizen voter probe lifted, then restored in legal boomerang

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter discusses federal subpoenas issued to California election workers, a dispute over more than 20,000 flagged mail-in ballots and the Justice Department's possible Supreme Court appeal ahead of the midterms.

A federal appeals court briefly lifted a block on the Trump administration’s efforts to investigate alleged voting by noncitizens in California, then reversed course hours later, sending the dispute to the full 11-judge 9th Circuit for rehearing.

Earlier Monday night, a three-judge panel granted the Justice Department’s request to pause a temporary restraining order issued by a San Francisco federal judge. That order had barred the administration from making further requests to set aside ballots under the warning of prosecution of state and local election officials who declined.

The panel said the government was likely to prevail in arguing that its requests and criminal investigations were core executive functions.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS

Hours later, the full 9th Circuit vacated the ruling and ordered the case reheard by all 11 active judges, according to the court’s order. The move restored the district court’s restrictions while the full court considers the dispute.

"The TRO issued by a San Francisco judge purporting to restrict DOJ investigations into election officials has been appropriately lifted," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on X before the temporary restraining order was restored. "Conducting criminal investigations is a core function of the executive branch, not the judiciary."

The case against the investigation of alleged noncitizen voting was brought by labor unions and civil rights groups, including the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens. They argued that DOJ and Homeland Security letters to election officials, which warned of potential criminal liability over ballots linked to suspected noncitizens, amounted to intimidation.

CALIFORNIA ELECTION WORKERS HIT WITH CRIMINAL SUBPOENAS AS TRUMP DOJ TURNS UP HEAT IN VOTING SHOWDOWN

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli (right) is warning the state of California's election officials that refusing to obey federal law about not allowing the counting of legal votes could bring potential prosecution against them. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg; Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times)

The Trump administration argues that allowing illegal voting and halting investigative work could lead to prosecution for those involved.

"Americans deserve to have confidence in their elections," Essayli wrote late Monday night. "The courts have made it clear that the preferred remedy for election law violations is criminal prosecution. Building on Operation Protect the Vote, we will continue investigating and charging those who violate election laws or assist in their violation."

The appeals court whiplash followed a separate Supreme Court rejection of the Trump administration's effort to protect the vote Monday. The justices denied an emergency request to require California to set aside mail ballots from roughly 20,000 registered voters federal officials flagged as likely noncitizens.

BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD

"We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent ​McCotter wrote on X.

The administration had demanded that California separate any alleged unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be U.S. citizens through investigations that the state has rejected without review.

"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the Justice Department wrote in its request to the Supreme Court.

DHS OFFICIAL VOWS TO PROSECUTE AND DEPORT NONCITIZENS CAUGHT ILLEGALLY VOTING AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The DOJ has been forced into a legal Catch-22 where it has to watch votes be cast in California, even if they have alleged evidence of them being noncitizen voters, and then pursue legal action afterward.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that 63 people were charged with election crimes Monday.

"Today's announcement marks the largest surge of voter-fraud arrests since President [Donald] Trump returned to office," Blanche wrote in a statement. "These foreign nationals allegedly took advantage of the trust of the American people and flouted the laws that govern our nation’s elections. This Department of Justice will continue investigating and prosecuting voter fraud to restore confidence in our electoral system."

The DOJ has charged 195 illegal immigrants across 25 states with illegal voting and voter registration offenses in the past nine weeks. There have been charges against 239 people with voting fraud offenses since Trump returned to the White House, according to the DOJ.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

#6044. Don’t Go Backward on China Policy

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALI WYNE is Senior Research and Advocacy Adviser for U.S.-China Relations at the International Crisis Group.

RYAN HASS is Director of the John L. Thornton China Center and Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored long-standing sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States.

Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy would also be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the run-up to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security.

The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans.

Trump’s views on China are iconoclastic in Washington, and even at odds with other members of his own administration and party. Whereas most policymakers agree that China is the United States’ foremost strategic competitor, Trump has embraced a narrow conception of competition focused primarily on the size of China’s trade surplus and its export of chemicals used to make fentanyl. He also sees Xi less as a determined geopolitical foe than as a transactional business rival with whom he can negotiate to stabilize bilateral ties.

This judgment—that dealing with China can and should be nonideological and transactional—was also present in Trump’s first term in office. It even survived the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Trump, believing that Xi had exported the virus, empowered senior advisers to implement a hard-line approach to China that included challenging the legitimacy of Chinese Communist Party rule and openly calling for political change. But Trump’s core views did not dictate U.S. policy as greatly then as they do now because he had less command over his own administration during his first term and was less dominant over the Republican Party as a whole.

Trump has also been chastened into a more realistic appreciation of Beijing’s power. China is the only country in the world that stared down Trump’s April 2025 tariff barrage and forced him to retreat. In 2026, Beijing used Washington’s fear of a fresh economic rupture to deter Trump from targeting major Chinese banks as part of his global efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. Even as the president claims to be ushering in a new era of U.S. dominance, he has had to acknowledge China as a “near peer”—a designation that his administration codified in its 2025 National Security Strategy. Similarly, he has touted the prospect of a “G-2” of the United States and China, making allies and partners worry that he is privileging Beijing’s sensitivities over their concerns.

In some discrete areas, the Trump administration continues to view China through a competitive lens. For example, it is reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese rare-earth exports through initiatives such as Project Vault, an effort to stockpile critical minerals, and pressuring countries to forswear participation in Chinese-led artificial intelligence initiatives. And even as Trump lambastes allies and partners, alleging that they exploit U.S. beneficence, Washington is deepening its security cooperation with treaty allies in Asia, including Australia and the Philippines, and stepping up its training of troops in Taiwan.

Yet on balance, the president has been more conciliatory than competitive toward China. And with his other foreign policy goals—dominating the Western Hemisphere, pushing for regime change in Iran, and ending the war in Ukraine—vying for priority, Trump has devoted far less attention to the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship than many observers had expected when he retook office. His various retreats on China have left the United States worse off: he has undermined Washington’s leverage over Beijing while causing U.S. allies and partners to question whether they should align with a country that prefers a veneer of stability with China to coordinated efforts to address Chinese assertiveness abroad and repression at home.

Because Trump’s China policy places him at odds with much of the foreign policy bureaucracy and the vast majority of lawmakers, including those within his own party, there will likely be pent-up pressure to resume intense strategic competition with China. Candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination, in particular, will be tempted to pledge to take a tougher approach to Beijing, potentially including calls to curtail high-level diplomatic exchanges between U.S. and Chinese officials or adopt more expansive measures to limit China’s technological progress. But attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.

Most obvious, the nearly decadelong U.S. effort to slow Chinese innovation through sanctions, tariffs, and export controls is foundering. In AI, for example, Chinese companies are finding workarounds to such efforts and advancing their capabilities alongside those of their U.S. peers. Any sustainable attempt to limit technology access also requires multilateral cooperation; as Washington’s ties with many of its closest allies and partners fray, questions are mounting about whether any coalition can thwart Beijing’s technological strides and would be willing to bear the costs of trying to do so.

At the same time, China is widening its lead in sectors such as electric vehicles, advanced robots, and life sciences. Attempting to construct a technological moat around the United States is unlikely to help it regain its competitiveness. Instead, Washington will need to strike a better balance between mitigating the security risks of Chinese investment and collaboration and securing commercial benefits from Chinese knowledge and industry. The United States could gain from using the same technology transfer practices that China employed against U.S. companies starting in the late 1970s, when Washington led in many cutting-edge technologies. In battery manufacturing, for instance, U.S. firms would benefit from acquiring know-how from their Chinese competitors, and both countries would gain if their laboratories pooled capabilities to accelerate the discovery of cures to diseases such as cancer.

The United States also may not be able to pick up where it left off before Trump retook office because even its well-wishers no longer can treat his foreign policy as an aberration. He won a second term after losing in 2020, and he did so more decisively than in 2016. Although U.S. allies and partners would welcome a more multilateralist administration after Trump, they will find it difficult to overlook the possibility that aggressive unilateralism will periodically shape Washington’s foreign policy. Merely eschewing Trump’s crude bullying will not be enough to rebuild trust; his successor must avoid treating allies and partners as instruments of strategic competition.

Paradoxically, though, Trump’s mishandling of China policy has opened the political space for a new, more durable strategy to emerge. Previously, proponents of sustained high-level diplomacy between the United States and China were often dismissed as shortsighted, Chinese investment in the United States was seen as a Trojan horse, and critiques of zero-sum conceptions of bilateral relations were considered naive. But Trump’s actions have shifted the Overton window of what is possible, creating room for a wider variety of ways to work productively with China.

Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress have gradually resumed bipartisan visits to China. Even Secretary of State Marco Rubio, one of the foremost hawks during his time in the Senate, said in September that it would be “outrageous” for top U.S. and Chinese officials to avoid each other. Respected voices in Washington, including former senior Biden administration officials, are calling for some joint ventures with Chinese companies to help U.S. companies develop. And there is a growing recognition in both Congress and the White House that China’s steady accrual of power necessitates a more focused approach to competition.

There is also public support for a new China policy. Although many policymakers frame relations with Beijing as a competition to be won, most Americans regard it as a reality to be managed. In a July 2025 survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 53 percent of Americans wanted the United States to pursue “friendly cooperation and engagement with China”; it was the first time since 2019 that a majority of respondents had expressed that view. Young people are driving this shift. A January 2026 Pew poll found that only 32 percent of Republicans and ten percent of Democrats between the ages of 18 and 49 called China an enemy, compared with 55 percent and 18 percent, respectively, of those age 50 and older. A March 2026 survey by the Searchlight Institute, a center-left think tank, found that 62 percent of respondents between 18 and 34 wanted the United States to “cooperate with China and improve U.S.-China relations.”

A better China policy will begin by abandoning hollow admonitions to “win” the strategic competition with Beijing. Although China faces numerous internal challenges, including slowing productivity, an aging population, and mounting government debt, it also has powerful advantages, two of which have become undeniable in Trump’s second term: China’s dominance of supply chains that provide vital commodities to Americans and its stranglehold on rare earths that the U.S. automotive industry and defense industrial base need to function.

The next president should neither understate nor exaggerate Beijing’s trajectory; rather, as we have previously argued, Washington should consider it “an enduring yet constrained competitor.” The inescapable reality is that neither country can deliver any knockout blows against the other without doing grievous damage to itself. Both countries will remain interdependent and have to operate with awareness of their vulnerabilities to each other.

If the world’s two foremost powers are fated to compete over the terms of coexistence, they must redouble efforts to avoid a catastrophic confrontation. Washington will have to build trust with rightfully wary allies and partners if it is to shore up deterrence in Asia. It will also have to continue signaling to Beijing a willingness to take reciprocal steps to reduce the risk of incidents that could spiral out of control, such as accidental air or naval collisions. Such signaling will become ever more essential as AI rapidly advances. Protecting the U.S. homeland against AI misuse and misalignment will require Washington to coordinate with Beijing on guardrails for frontier models and reject the argument that such efforts are inimical to securing a decisive strategic advantage over China. The need to work together on AI safety is already shaping U.S.-Chinese relations: at September’s summit between Trump and Xi, the two countries agreed to establish an incident alert system, and many members of Congress have publicly supported broader bilateral efforts with China to reduce the risks of AI-enabled security crises.

Reindustrialization will also be a major project for Trump’s successor. Progress on that front will be essential if the United States is to reduce its vulnerabilities to China and put itself on firmer footing to pursue a favorable coexistence. The next Congress and potential 2028 candidates could outline realistic plans for reducing dependence on China for active pharmaceutical ingredients, rare earths, and potential future chokepoints. They could also prioritize key industries on which U.S. security depends, such as AI-powered robotics and shipbuilding, and explain how they would deploy funding and talent to those sectors. Elsewhere, with public support for the president’s tariffs sagging, his successor could narrow or place sunset provisions on—or, through executive order, rescind—protectionist policies toward China that lower productivity and increase the costs of inputs for American producers. Such efforts would be broadly politically popular at home and would better position the United States to work with allies and partners to push back on China’s unfair economic practices, including extensive subsidies, undervalued currency, and suppressed domestic demand.

Ultimately, the United States must remember that its external competitiveness will flow from its internal vigor. Leaders in Washington should accordingly embed policy positions on China in a hopeful vision: helping the United States realize its potential as a pluralistic, self-correcting democracy. Framing U.S.-Chinese relations around the United States’ capacity to steer its ties with China in productive directions is more likely to produce a resilient approach than casting Washington as a victim or reasserting a policy framework that no longer meets the moment.

Observers can and should debate specific policy positions vigorously. But another harsh swing in the United States’ approach to China would create more policy instability while also discounting the extent to which Beijing’s rise is transforming the geopolitical balance. Taking advantage of the political space that Trump has generated, however ineptly, the new Congress taking office after the 2026 midterms and presidential aspirants looking to run in 2028 will have an opportunity to present a steadier approach, articulating a clear focus on national renewal and a balanced posture toward Beijing that reflects the mood of the American public. Approaching China’s challenge with this sensibility would not only be more prescriptively sound; it would also be more politically sustainable.

How America Can Take Advantage of the Status Quo

Why the United States Should Not Overreact to China and Russia

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Niall Ferguson, Lisa Klaassen, and Eric Schmidt

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

Theodore Bunzel, Edward Fishman, and Addar Levi

#6042. Soviet Nostalgia Is a Geopolitical Dead End

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Soviet Nostalgia Is a Geopolitical Dead End

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Across the former Soviet Union and its satellite states, almost everyone knows The Irony of Fate, a 1976 romantic comedy in which a Moscow surgeon gets drunk at a bathhouse on New Year’s Eve and ends up on a plane to Leningrad. He gives a taxi driver his Moscow address, “Third Builder’s Street,” and arrives at an identical block of flats, where his key opens the door.

The world that the movie describes was once much larger than Russia itself. You could arrive in Kyiv, Tbilisi, or Riga and speak Russian; quote the same Soviet films; laugh at the same jokes; and assume that underneath all the flags, languages, and newly drawn borders there was still some common social and cultural space holding the place together.

Across the former Soviet Union and its satellite states, almost everyone knows The Irony of Fate, a 1976 romantic comedy in which a Moscow surgeon gets drunk at a bathhouse on New Year’s Eve and ends up on a plane to Leningrad. He gives a taxi driver his Moscow address, “Third Builder’s Street,” and arrives at an identical block of flats, where his key opens the door.

The world that the movie describes was once much larger than Russia itself. You could arrive in Kyiv, Tbilisi, or Riga and speak Russian; quote the same Soviet films; laugh at the same jokes; and assume that underneath all the flags, languages, and newly drawn borders there was still some common social and cultural space holding the place together.

When Russia set out to restore that world by force, some of its nostalgic talking points, once confined to state television, found a wide company in the West. Tucker Carlson, who has turned it into a routine, tells his audience that Ukraine is weak, corrupt, and finished. Candace Owens flew to Russia and came back saying, “they are lying to us about Russia.” Others, such as U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, refuse to support aid for a country defending itself from invasion.

John Mearsheimer and Noam Chomsky have built long careers explaining that whatever Russia does is somebody else’s fault. Francesca Albanese, a U.N. special rapporteur, has called for an end to arms deliveries to a country fighting against an invader.

The left and the right rarely agree on anything, yet here, some of their thinkers converge: Sooner or later, Kyiv must learn to live with Moscow’s demands. Whether it’s Owen Matthews writing in the Spectator that Ukraine is losing the war or Jeffrey Sachs insisting that Kyiv will never join NATO, the underlying belief is the same. For some people shaped by that world, its disappearance is sad. There is a little of Anton Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard in them: They are so attached to the estate that they can scarcely imagine a world beyond it.

Leaving Russia for the West did not always mean leaving its imperial assumptions behind. Joseph Brodsky, persecuted and exiled by the Soviet state, greeted Ukrainian independence with a poem full of insults, imagining Ukrainians returning to Russian poet Alexander Pushkin on their deathbeds rather than their own Taras Shevchenko. Pushkin himself, in “To the Slanderers of Russia,” told Europe to stay out of what he presented as a family quarrel among Slavs during Russia’s suppression of the Polish uprising in 1831.

What is striking is how many people who never lived in that world have arrived at the same conclusion. These pundits identify Ukraine’s problems well. Kyiv is short of men, money, and Patriot interceptors; corruption persists; and its allies’ declarations have far outrun their policies. They are right about the diagnosis and wrong about the cure.

They also exaggerate the threat. Russia has advanced at enormous cost to Ukraine, yet a snail set off from its starting positions might have reached parts of today’s front line first. Ukraine won the decisive battle for Kyiv, when Moscow’s aim was a disarmed Ukraine under a government of its choosing. It need not recover all its territory to win. If it remains sovereign, secure, and in the West, then Russia’s larger project will have failed. The only real Russian victory is the one that these arguments point toward—a Ukraine that is left vulnerable and subject to Moscow’s will.

The worst part of this so-called realist take is the claim that it is for Ukraine’s own good. By the forecasts of these observers, Ukraine was supposed to lose in 2022, then every year since. Instead of revising the premise, they move the date forward and wait for history to rescue the thinking.

Even the more serious skeptics concede that Russian President Vladimir Putin has not changed his war aims and that U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner is naive to think that business deals will seduce the Kremlin into peace. If Putin cannot be persuaded, what is Ukraine supposed to negotiate? A concession to a man who demands the maximum will only be a down payment. Georgia learned this the hard way. Its 2008 cease-fire with Russia was followed by the latter’s invasion of Crimea; the Minsk agreements were followed by the full-scale invasion.

Another argument that keeps resurfacing is that the West provoked the war. Mearsheimer and Chomsky describe Russian aggression as a response to a menacing NATO, the supposed existential threat that Putin cites and his Western interpreters obligingly repeat. Yet Moscow was already using force in Moldova and Georgia in the early 1990s, when NATO enlargement was hardly an available excuse. You can call those ethnic conflicts, as some do, but after so many Russian acts of aggression, ignoring the reality takes real determination. The only power that has invaded anyone in the neighborhood is Russia. NATO only prevents it from doing so.

What runs through all this is an old fatalism, very familiar in Russia, in which Russian power is a constant, Western resolve is fickle, and Ukrainian resistance is doomed. It calls itself realism, but it is really pessimism, in which history can change everything except Russia’s behavior. It treats Moscow’s desires as objective reality and Ukraine’s goals as childish aspirations, in the spirit of the Brezhnev Doctrine, where small countries choose freely, provided that Moscow approves.

Soviet power once looked equally permanent; in Alexei Yurchak’s words, “everything was forever, until it was no more.” The Baltic states were told that Russia would never tolerate their joining NATO. They did not move on the map. The policy and debate did, because Western governments decided it should. Yes, they joined while Russia was weak. That is exactly the point.

If Western policy has failed, then the policy should change. If Ukraine lacks air defense, the answer is more air defense. Pressure on Russia should grow until Moscow understands that the West will hold its ground and that the war will end as a strategic loss even if Russia takes the rest of the Donbas, which it does not really need. That means guaranteeing Ukraine’s future security and denying Moscow that lever. Is there a Western consensus on this yet? No. Let’s hope one arrives, because otherwise the problems will end up far closer to home.

Why, then, does the argument keep returning? For some, it is a hatred of the West so complete that every war turns into a story about American wrongdoing. For others, it is audience. Outrage and fringe arguments sell, and Moscow makes a good backdrop for a story about Western decline. And for more than a few, it is simply clear sympathy for Russia, for its strongman, its bigotry framed as tradition, its fantasy of itself as the third Rome against a decadent West.

Then for others, it is fear. In my village in the mountains of Georgia, my neighbor, a man called Valeri, says much the same thing as these commentators, though one should be more forgiving of Valeri. Russian troops already occupy part of his country, and one morning, he may discover that his barn is on the Russian side of the line. When he says that Russia is too big and too dangerous, one can understand. His is a foreign policy of the village bench. But the same worldview, minus the cows, turns up in American studios and newspapers, among people who know that they have more choices.

Whether they echo that view from Moscow or in the West, they will find the Ukraine that comes out of this war even harder to recognize. Young Ukrainians speak more Ukrainian, consume less Russian culture, and understand fewer of the Soviet references that once traveled from Moscow to Mykolaiv. After generations of Russification, the recovery of a national consciousness is not an easy task. It may come with mistakes. But a country bombed in the name of a supposedly common history, that took tyranny and bloodshed to hold together, cannot be expected to preserve that history for the comfort of people who remember it fondly.

Putin can drop more bombs and probably will, but after nearly five years of war, it is hard to imagine Ukrainians deciding that capitulation is the answer. Like other empires, the Russian one will sooner or later collapse, including in people’s heads. Along with it will go the longing to walk into Kyiv or Tbilisi and expect the keys to fit.

Ani Chkhikvadze is a Georgian reporter based in Washington.

#6041. Michigan voters weigh in after Dem Rep Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate

Will Republicans' Haley Stevens gambit pay off?

OAKLAND COUNTY, MICHIGAN — Michigan’s Republican ticket had a clear message for voters preparing to vote in the midterm elections: Their path to victory relies on winning over voters who typically don’t align themselves with the GOP.

That prospect appeared to be buoyed by Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th-hour endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed. Early Monday afternoon, Republican operatives in Michigan blasted out a press release advertising an event just hours later intended to tout Stevens’ endorsement and its purported impact on Black and Jewish voters.

In front of a throng of press at the Michigan GOP’s headquarters, six community leaders representing African Americans and Jews criticized what they saw as El-Sayed’s excesses and lauded Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers. Broadly, they argued that El-Sayed had insufficiently distanced himself from some of his radical associations, that Stevens' endorsement had real significance for the race and that they were seeing an unprecedented groundswell of support for Republicans among their peers.

MIKE ROGERS DISHES ON HOW SHOCK HALEY STEVENS ENDORSEMENT UNFOLDED HOURS BEFORE ELECTION DAY

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and U.S. Senate candidate, and Rep. Haley Stevens, a Democrat from Michigan, speak to members of the media following a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit, Mich., on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, formally backed Rogers, sealing her rupture with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In addition to the community leaders, close to two dozen others — many of whom were Black or Jewish — attended the event as well. While some political observers have cast doubt on the impact of Stevens' endorsement and the degree to which African Americans and Jews are defecting from the Democratic Party, members of those communities told Fox News Digital the shift is happening.

"I believe it's going to make a big difference that she came out," Michelle Nard, an African American former Democrat running for state Senate, told Fox News Digital. "She had a big following. She's a great congresswoman, a great state representative for the United States."

BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’

Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens appears alongside GOP rival Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Nov. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Rogers for Senate)

Nard recounted how she had recently spoken to a Black woman who highlighted that her community makes a big deal of going to the polls on Election Day, a point she used to stress that Haley’s endorsement, though late in the cycle, could still influence last-second voters.

"You have strong Haley Stevens supporters in our community that will support her to the end, and then you have some that feel betrayed," Marcus Bowman, a metro Detroit school board trustee, told Fox News Digital.

Bowman, who says he knows Stevens personally, said: "True supporters of Haley Stevens, they know her as a person and they know what she represents. I think they will follow her and respect her for her decision based off some of the radical things we've heard about Abdul El-Sayed."

While those who spoke were handpicked for a Republican news conference, there is some data to back up Black voter defection. Between August and September, El-Sayed’s support among African Americans held steady at around 75%, well below the party's typical benchmark.

FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and former Wayne County Health Department Director Abdul El-Sayed are facing off in the August 4, 2026, Democratic Senate primary in the Great Lakes battleground state. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The Arab American community in the Detroit metropolitan area has historically been at odds with African Americans in the areas across a number of issues, a theme that has come up occasionally during El-Sayed’s campaign.

While comparable polls have not found similar trends among Jewish voters, who are a much smaller part of Michigan’s electorate, a number of high-profile members of the communities, including top donors, have flocked to the Rogers camp.

"Haley, what she did was give a lot of Jews permission, hardcore left-wing Democrats, permission to now say, you know what, if Haley can endorse him, I can vote for him," Aaron Tobin, a conservative Jewish community leader, told Fox News Digital in reference to Mike Rogers. "Now I think she's broken that wall down, and now they can see that a hardcore Democrat — and she was very successful and very popular in Michigan — if she said Mike Rogers is good enough for her, I think a lot of Jews are going to say, 'I'm going to vote for him because Abdul just says the worst things.'"

Ezra, another Jewish voter, told Fox News Digital that he believes Jews have increasingly been abandoned by the Democratic Party and, even if Stevens’ endorsement doesn’t move the needle, he’s grateful that she took a stand.

"The [March 12] terrorist attack in [a] West Bloomfield [synagogue], I believe was the starting point of the Detroit Jewish community being afraid and that fear was not alleviated over the next [six months]. That fear has not been alleviated by Abdul El-Sayed in any sort of way, which is why I think you're seeing this," he said. "We're waiting for something and it's not coming. And so that's why I think you're seeing so many in the Jewish community moving for Mike Rogers because they're like, you know what, that guy's going to keep my family safe. The other guy's not."

MAMDANI, HASAN PIKER AMONG RADICAL LEFT-WING VOICES ERUPTING OVER HALEY STEVENS' ENDORSEMENT SWITCH

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, announces support from Democrats as he launches a 'Dems for Mike' coalition, on August 20, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

"I think in some ways, it's, it's more brave because it's at the last minute. In some ways, you know what, who knows, even if it, if it's 100 votes or 1000 votes, then it makes a difference," he added.

These alleged breakthroughs with traditionally Democratic constituencies took center stage at Rogers’ closing rally on Monday night. At one point, the campaign invited six Black and Jewish voters, most of them former Democrats, to take the stage where they explained why they believed El-Sayed to be too extreme for their support. Rogers himself praised the group during his final campaign speech, invoked the need for unity and thanked Stevens at length for her endorsement.

Conservatives at the rally were clearly grateful to Stevens for her endorsement, with nearly every mention of her name being met with cheers or chants of her name. Republicans are even optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement could trickle down to their down-ballot races.

MICHIGAN DEM CLAIMS STEVENS SHOT DOWN ROGERS ENDORSEMENT RUMOR HOURS BEFORE TURNING ON EL-SAYED

Detroit voters at the polls inside Central United Methodist Church on Nov. 5, 2024 in downtown Detroit, Mich. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

"I was on the ground last week in Michigan and Ohio, and the momentum in Michigan is real. It was real before Haley Stevens endorsed Mike Rogers, even more real now," Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, told Fox News Digital.

Piper said he "absolutely" believes Stevens’ endorsement will move the needle for Michigan Republican attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd.

"You know, around the Detroit area, Grosse Pointe, Detroit, elsewhere, I saw homemade yard signs in the yards of Black churches that said African Americans and Jews stand together. And that was powerful."

Lloyd said he is optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers could give him a boost.

"Well, I saw something today in the news that basically said 50% of the available voters have voted through absentee and early voting. We still have one day left. And as we've said, you know, the race isn't done until 8 o'clock tomorrow night when the polls close," he said. "So, if this made a difference for someone who had been sitting on the sideline and they decided they were going to get out and vote because of it, I'm excited for that."

Democrats have argued Stevens’ endorsement could strengthen, rather than weaken, El-Sayed’s support. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said he expected the episode to galvanize Democrats, while El-Sayed’s campaign reported raising $2.4 million Sunday, its largest fundraising day of the campaign.

While cutting into the Democratic Party’s margins by successfully pulling away Black and Jewish voters could prove valuable to the GOP, a reversion among Arab voters — who swung toward Republicans in 2024 but strongly favor El-Sayed — could erase such gains. Fox News’ final power ranking rated Michigan’s Senate race as a toss-up, meaning that, as voters head to the polls, neither party holds a clear edge.
